summary.en: Psychedelic music grew out of the use of the hallucinogen LSD. That use was certainly hedonistic, but it was also tied, to a degree, to the countercultural social currents of the time.
summary.zh: 迷幻音乐源自于致幻药物LSD的使用。这种使用当然带有享乐性质，但一定程度上也与反主流文化之社会思潮有所关联。

body.zh:
迷幻音乐源自于致幻药物LSD的使用。这种使用当然带有享乐性质，但一定程度上也与反主流文化之社会思潮有所关联。

眼下来到了课程的第七章，《摇滚史》第一部分的最后一章。我们将要讨论迷幻时期，后者一般囊括从1966年到1969年的日子，也即1960年代的最末期。在书中，我称之为“高峰与创想”。大家回想一下是如何走到这个节点的吧。我们讲过英伦入侵，The Beatles在1964年2月到访美国后，掀起了英伦音乐的风潮。我们也谈过美国的回应，1965年夏天，The Byrds和Bob Dylan对英伦入侵予以反击，并促成了folk rock及类似作品的兴起。之后，我们提到了Motown和Stax在同期的崛起，以及那段时间里的黑人流行乐场景。那么从1966年起，除了上面提及的各种流派，我们还能看见逐渐崛起的迷幻摇滚场景。

开始讲述本章内容之前，我想先谈谈与之相关的一些概念。首先是主流与亚文化的对立。音乐学者喜欢研究亚文化，因为它表明了主流之外仍存在着活跃的音乐场景。例如，在本章课程中，我们将谈到旧金山的迷幻亚文化以及伦敦的类似圈子。在最初的一两年里，迷幻音乐几乎就是地下的产物；若想知道个中情况，就只能亲临现场以一探究竟。虽然它有时会登上媒体，但说到底并不属于主流。所谓主流艺人，是在全国乃至国际的大众视野之下做些事情；相对地，那些在暗处发展的艺人，例如涉及迷幻运动、迷幻音乐者，就属于亚文化的范畴。我们会在主流艺人与亚文化艺人之间作个划分，并聊聊旧金山和伦敦的亚文化；一定程度上，也会牵涉到洛杉矶。

其次是音乐野心的膨胀，以及我称之为嬉皮士美学(hippie aesthetic)的理念的形成。这个概念出现于50年代末及60年代。对于音乐应当何为，当时部分音乐人的野心与日俱增。音乐开始成为更加重要的艺术表达、艺术创造的途径，而非纸巾、纸杯那类用完即弃的一次性制品。他们对自己的音乐有了更多大胆的设想，并试图使之变成真正的艺术。前几章提及The Beatles、The Beach Boys和Dylan时，我们也谈过这一点。

以上就是一些有关概念。我们也会思考一个问题：音乐怎能变得“迷幻”呢？药物确实能够致幻，但音乐何以如此？在此要区分的，是“在药物陪伴下聆听的音乐”与“自身即有迷幻感觉的音乐”。

上述主题将贯穿本章。那么现在开始吧，先讲讲LSD(迷幻药)的兴起。说到迷幻，当然不能略过药物的问题。但不要以为我在支持用药或者鼓励各位去尝试，绝对不是那样。我们只是作为历史研究者来客观地探讨其来龙去脉。虽说当时流传着不少种类的毒品，但LSD是最受关注的一种，因为其致幻效果与反主流文化的思想、审美相适配（至少它的拥趸如此认为）。LSD由瑞士化学家Albert Hoffmann于1943年合成。当时他正在探索偏头痛的疗法，因此在实验室里制备了这种药方。他并没有直接服用LSD，而是通过皮肤接触吸收了制剂成分。他可能没意识到这件事，但话说回来，就算他察觉了，情况又能有多糟糕呢？说不定他从此就克服了偏头痛，那正是他的研发目标。科学家要与大量药物打交道，其中大多数最终都没有成效，所以他可能对LSD没有什么防备。常言道，谁能辨真假。很多东西都是可疑的，并且为人夸大，但那天下班的时候，实验助理发现他的举止有点奇怪。两人都是以单车为通勤方式，出于安全考虑，助理觉得最好跟着他。显然，归家路上，LSD开始起效了。据Albert Hoffmann本人回忆，当时他行进得很慢，那地平线在不断浮动，一切都变得五彩缤纷。所有事情都像发生在慢镜头里一样。而根据助理的描述，他在单车上处于发狂状态。这实际上是首例LSD“神游”（LSD trip）。Albert Hoffman把他的发现写了下来，并认为这种药的效果有潜在的用处。美国中情局介入其中，以为这是让人说真话的麻醉药，可以用在俄罗斯间谍身上、让他们泄露秘密。精神病医生也曾动了心思，觉得如果用量较低，它或许可以用于治疗酗酒。总之，当时只有情报部门和医药界知道这种药物的存在，因为它是作为科学发现而被记录在案的。

我们会花点时间讲一下Timothy Leary这个人，他是知晓LSD之本质的科学家之一。事实上，直到1966年10月，LSD都是完全合法的药物，因为人们并不把它视为威胁。当时它只是一种医疗用药。LSD最初是在加州遭到禁用，之后美国的其余地方也效仿了。缘由之一在于，了解LSD及其享乐用途的人——上层人士，如医生、牙医以及同一社交圈里的律师或商人——不时把LSD当作餐后咖啡的陪衬。他们服下药品，开始“神游”。只要服用时身处封闭的空间，大家就不觉得有太大危险。The Beatles（至少John Lennon和George Harrison两位成员）可以说是大牌乐队里最早的受害者。事情发生在1965年初，John和George带着他们的妻子去和相识的英国牙医聚餐。牙医私自在咖啡里加了一点LSD，于是所有人都开始“神游”了。其实，最初药物还没起效时，那个牙医就不断问他们：“现在感觉如何？如何？”这有点吓到他们了，他们以为他图谋不轨。所以他们决定离开，而就在车上，LSD突然起效了，余下整晚都是彻底的“神游”。The Beatles可能还挺喜欢LSD，因为之后他们又多次服用了它。但话说回来，他们接触LSD的途径仍是上层人士的派对。我们讲过，The Beatles在1965年初接触了LSD，而Paul McCartney是最晚加入的一个。在1967年的“爱之夏”（summer of love）之前，我们都没有频繁地听到关于LSD的新闻，类似事件基本都是悄悄发生的。

那么，人们为什么要服用LSD呢？我们已经明白了它的药效，但其代表的价值观是什么？其中一项自然是享乐，世上有大量的瘾君子只想着麻痹自己、消遣一番。不过，LSD还真的被当作反主流文化的工具。它与更高的观念相结合，那就是服用LSD有助于打破以服从社会规矩乃至谎言的方式来铸造的壁垒。所以服用LSD有助于做回自己，重获本真；这或许被你从小遵照的现代社会规则所否定。由此，它是一条通往智慧和更高观念的途径。这刚好与60年代末嬉皮士拥护的反主流文化概念相符，也即自行创造一种不会重蹈长辈之覆辙的文化。父母、老师、政府和教会都在撒谎，要想找回真相，LSD可能就是那灵丹妙药，能够帮助你调整内心、看见真理。当然，LSD的使用催生了“神游”（the trip）这一概念，因为LSD的体验往往呈现为一趟旅程。但“旅程”一词常在反主流文化的语境下出现，所以如果某人经历了一趟“剧烈的旅程”，其可能是货真价实的LSD“神游”，也可能单纯是非常糟糕的生理体验。我可能会讲讲某个名人的“神游”经历。这就是“神游”的概念。

可以想见，音乐将以两种方式介入“神游”。音乐能够强化LSD“神游”的体验，也可以说是药物体验的佐料。Ken Kesey和the Merry Pranksters大概就是这么做的，我们会在下一节中提到他们。但音乐本身也可以成为独立的“神游”途径，无需借助LSD或其他药物。为此，音乐必须变得更概念化，更大胆，更严肃；当然，篇幅上也要更长，以便带你深入“神游”状态。有趣的是，在这些以精神性音乐作“神游”的嬉皮士身上，重现了对于绝对音乐（absolute music）的偏好——这种态度曾盛行于19世纪的欧洲艺术音乐的圈子。人们曾以同样的口吻谈论贝多芬的交响曲。

在下一节中，我们将聚焦于音乐如何变得严肃且富有野心——如果音乐本身会引发“神游”，或至少强化“神游”的体验，那么音乐是如何为此作出改变的呢？这将是下一节的内容。
body.en:
Psychedelic music grew out of the use of the hallucinogen LSD. That use was certainly hedonistic, but it was also tied, to a degree, to the countercultural social currents of the time.

We have now reached Chapter 7—the last chapter of Part One of History of Rock. We will discuss the psychedelic period, generally covering 1966 through 1969, the very end of the 1960s. In the book I call it “peaks and experiments.” Recall how we got here. We covered the British Invasion: after the Beatles visited the U.S. in February 1964, British music took off. We also covered America’s reply: in the summer of 1965 the Byrds and Bob Dylan pushed back against the Invasion and helped folk rock and related styles rise. Then we looked at Motown and Stax rising in the same years, and at the Black popular-music scene of that stretch. From 1966 on, alongside those styles, a psychedelic rock scene gradually takes shape.

Before the chapter proper, a few related ideas. First, mainstream versus subculture. Music scholars like subcultures because they show active scenes outside the mainstream. In this chapter we will talk about San Francisco’s psychedelic subculture and a similar circle in London. For the first year or two, psychedelic music was almost entirely underground; to know what was going on, you had to be there. It sometimes made the press, but it was not mainstream. Mainstream artists work in national or international public view; artists developing in the shadows—those tied to the psychedelic movement and its music—belong to subculture. We will draw a line between mainstream and subcultural artists, talk about San Francisco and London, and to some extent Los Angeles.

Second, the swelling of musical ambition, and what I call the hippie aesthetic. That idea takes shape in the late 1950s and the 1960s. For some musicians, ambition about what music should do grew day by day. Music became a more important path of artistic expression and creation—not a disposable product like paper tissues or paper cups. They made bolder plans for their music and tried to turn it into real art. We already touched this when we discussed the Beatles, the Beach Boys, and Dylan in earlier chapters.

Those are the framing ideas. We will also ask: how can music itself become “psychedelic”? Drugs can hallucinate—but how can music? Distinguish music heard while on drugs from music that itself feels psychedelic.

Those themes run through the chapter. We begin with the rise of LSD. You cannot talk psychedelia without drugs. I am not endorsing or encouraging use—absolutely not. We discuss it as historians, objectively. Many drugs circulated then, but LSD drew the most attention because its effects seemed to fit countercultural ideas and aesthetics (at least as its advocates saw them). Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann synthesized LSD in 1943 while exploring migraine treatments. He did not take it deliberately; he absorbed it through skin contact. He may not have realized it—and even if he had, how bad could it be? Perhaps it would cure his migraine, which was the goal. Scientists handle many compounds; most go nowhere, so he may not have been wary. As the saying goes, who can tell truth from rumor. Much is doubtful and exaggerated, but at the end of that day an assistant noticed his odd behavior. Both cycled home; for safety the assistant followed. On the way home LSD clearly took hold. Hofmann later recalled moving very slowly, the horizon floating, everything vivid with color, as if in slow motion. The assistant described him as frantic on the bicycle. That was the first LSD trip. Hofmann wrote up the discovery and thought the drug might be useful. The CIA got involved, hoping it was a truth serum for Soviet spies. Psychiatrists wondered whether low doses might treat alcoholism. For a time only intelligence and medicine knew of it, because it was recorded as a scientific find.

We will spend a little on Timothy Leary, one of the scientists who understood LSD’s nature. In fact until October 1966 LSD was fully legal—people did not treat it as a threat. It was a medical drug. It was first banned in California, then elsewhere in the U.S. One reason: people who knew LSD’s recreational use—upper-class circles of doctors, dentists, and lawyers or businessmen in the same set—sometimes took it like an after-dinner coffee. They took the drug and “tripped.” In a closed space, it did not feel especially dangerous. The Beatles—at least John Lennon and George Harrison—were among the first major-band casualties. In early 1965 John and George and their wives dined with a British dentist they knew. He slipped LSD into the coffee; everyone started to trip. At first, before it hit, the dentist kept asking “How do you feel? How?” which spooked them—they thought he had designs. They left; in the car LSD suddenly kicked in, and the rest of the night was a full trip. The Beatles may have liked LSD; they took it again later. But their path to it was still those upper-class parties. We said they met LSD in early 1965; Paul McCartney was last to join. Before the 1967 Summer of Love we did not hear much about LSD in the news; such events mostly stayed quiet.

Why take LSD? We know the effects—but what values did it stand for? One is plainly pleasure; many users only want to numb out and have fun. Yet LSD was also treated as a countercultural tool. It joined a higher idea: that LSD helps break walls built by obeying social rules and even lies. So taking LSD helps you become yourself again, recover authenticity that modern social rules may have denied you since childhood. It becomes a path to wisdom and higher ideas. That fits late-1960s hippie counterculture: invent a culture that will not repeat the elders’ mistakes. Parents, teachers, government, and church all lie; to find truth, LSD might be the remedy that resets the mind and lets you see. LSD use also produced the idea of “the trip,” because the experience often felt like a journey. “Journey” was common countercultural language, so a “heavy trip” might be a real LSD trip or simply a very bad physical experience. I may mention some famous people’s trips. That is the concept of the trip.

Music enters the trip in two ways. It can intensify an LSD trip—seasoning for the drug experience. Ken Kesey and the Merry Pranksters roughly worked that way; we will meet them next. But music can also be a trip on its own, without LSD or other drugs. For that, music must become more conceptual, bolder, more serious—and longer, so it can carry you deep into the trip. Interestingly, among hippies who used spiritual music as a trip, a preference for absolute music returned—an attitude once common in nineteenth-century European art-music circles. People once spoke of Beethoven’s symphonies in the same tone.

Next section we focus on how music grew serious and ambitious—if music itself triggers a “trip,” or at least intensifies one, how does music change to do that? That is next.
